knowledge_graph.title: Williams syndrome
knowledge_graph.description: Williams syndrome, also Williams–Beuren syndrome, is a genetic disorder that affects many parts of the body. Facial features frequently include a broad forehead, underdeveloped chin, short nose, and full cheeks.

related_questions.question: What is the life expectancy of a person with Williams syndrome?
related_questions.snippet: Most people with Williams syndrome have a normal life expectancy, but some may have a reduced life expectancy due to complications of the disease (such as cardiovascular problems). Oftentimes, people with Williams syndrome will need additional support as they grow into adults.
related_questions.title: Williams syndrome - Cleveland Clinic

related_questions.question: What is the cause of Williams syndrome?
related_questions.snippet: Williams syndrome is caused by the loss (deletion ) of genetic material from a specific region of chromosome 7. The deleted region includes 25 to 27 genes, and researchers believe that a loss of several of these genes contributes to the characteristic features of this disorder.
related_questions.title: Williams syndrome: MedlinePlus Genetics

related_questions.question: Can adults with Williams syndrome live on their own?
related_questions.snippet: The prognosis for individuals with WS varies. Some degree of impaired intellect is found in most people with the disorder. Some adults are able to function independently, complete academic or vocational school, and live in supervised homes or on their own; most live with a caregiver.
related_questions.title: Williams Syndrome - BrainFacts

related_questions.question: Can Williams syndrome be cured?
related_questions.snippet: How is Williams syndrome treated? There is no specific cure for Williams syndrome, so care is focused on treating specific symptoms or cardiovascular problems.
related_questions.title: Williams Syndrome | Boston Children's Hospital

text_blocks.snippet: Williams syndrome, not Williamson disease, is a rare genetic disorder characterized by distinctive facial features, cardiovascular problems, developmental delays, and a unique personality. It's caused by a deletion of genes on chromosome 7, and individuals with the condition often exhibit an overly friendly, sociable demeanor and a love for music.
snippet_highlighted_words: a rare genetic disorder characterized by distinctive facial features, cardiovascular problems, developmental delays, and a unique personality

list.title: Facial Features:
list.snippet: Often described as "elfin-like," with a wide mouth, full lips, a short nose, and puffy eyes.

list.title: Cardiovascular Issues:
list.snippet: Many individuals with Williams syndrome have heart defects, particularly supravalvular aortic stenosis (narrowing of the aorta).

list.title: Developmental Delays:
list.snippet: Developmental delays are common, and some individuals may experience intellectual disability.

list.title: Personality:
list.snippet: People with Williams syndrome are often described as overly friendly, sociable, and have a strong affinity for music.

list.title: Connective Tissue:
list.snippet: Connective tissue abnormalities can lead to joint problems, and some individuals may have loose skin.

list.title: Other Symptoms:
list.snippet: Short stature, feeding difficulties, and hyperacusis (sensitivity to loud noises) can also occur.

text_blocks.snippet: Williams syndrome is caused by a deletion of genes on chromosome 7, specifically in the "Williams syndrome critical region" at 7q11.23. This deletion typically occurs spontaneously at the time of conception.
Diagnosis is usually made through a combination of physical examination, developmental assessment, and genetic testing (usually a FISH test or microarray) to identify the deletion on chromosome 7.
While there's no cure, treatments focus on managing symptoms and improving quality of life. This may include:

list.snippet: Cardiovascular care: Monitoring and treating heart defects.
Physical and occupational therapy: Addressing developmental delays and motor skills.
Speech therapy: Helping with speech and language development.
Educational support: Providing appropriate educational interventions.
